opening_question_spark: If water can crush an air pocket, why not your whole body?
entry_transition: Most of your body is water, which barely compresses.
cta: How deep would you dare to go?
body: Water-rich tissue changes very little under pressure.
Air in ears and sinuses shrinks much more.
Pressure rises about one atmosphere every ten meters.
At ten meters, total pressure is about double.
Unequal pressure can injure those air-filled spaces.
Underwater breathing would remove the limit of running out of air.
But it would not remove pressure from your body.
At extreme depths, high pressure can disturb normal nerve function.
So there is no fixed human depth set by breathing alone.
optional_closing: Breathing solves one problem, not every pressure problem.
full_narration: If water can crush an air pocket, why not your whole body? Most of your body is water, which barely compresses. Water-rich tissue changes very little under pressure. Air in ears and sinuses shrinks much more. Pressure rises about one atmosphere every ten meters. At ten meters, total pressure is about double. Unequal pressure can injure those air-filled spaces. Underwater breathing would remove the limit of running out of air. But it would not remove pressure from your body. At extreme depths, high pressure can disturb normal nerve function. So there is no fixed human depth set by breathing alone. Breathing solves one problem, not every pressure problem. How deep would you dare to go?
